prompt: Is it better to have a few close friends or many casual ones? Write an essay with a clear position.
text:
# A Few Close Friends Beat Many Casual Ones

If I had to choose between a few close friends and many casual ones, I would choose the few. Casual friends are pleasant, and I'm not arguing against them. But the things that make friendship valuable come almost entirely from closeness.

## What close friends give you

The first thing is support when life goes badly. When you lose a job, face a diagnosis, or end a marriage, you need someone who will pick up the phone at midnight, and casual friends rarely do that. They like you, but they don't know your history well enough to help, and neither of you expects the relationship to carry that weight.

The second is honesty. A close friend can tell you that you're making a mistake, and you will listen because you know they care about you. A casual friend who says the same thing sounds like an intrusion, so most casual friends say nothing. Their company is easy partly because it asks so little of either person.

The third is being known. Most of us want at least one or two people who understand us as we really are, including our flaws. That kind of knowing takes years of shared time, and it can't be spread across fifty people.

## The evidence points the same way

Research on well-being supports this. Studies of adult development, such as the long-running Harvard study, have found that the quality of people's close relationships predicts their health and happiness in later life better than the number of their social contacts does. People with a few warm, dependable relationships tend to do well. People with large networks but no one to confide in often report loneliness.

There is also a limit on how many close ties a person can keep. Time and attention are finite. The anthropologist Robin Dunbar has estimated that people can sustain only about five intimate relationships and about fifteen good friendships. Each friend you add costs time you would otherwise spend on the people who matter most. If you spread yourself across a hundred acquaintances, you will likely have little left for the three people who would show up at your hospital bed.

## The case for casual friends

The best argument for many casual friends is that they bring variety. Sociologist Mark Granovetter showed that "weak ties" are often how people hear about jobs, ideas and opportunities, because acquaintances move in circles that our close friends don't. Casual friends also make daily life warmer. A friendly neighbor, a regular at the gym, or a colleague you chat with all add small pleasures that are easy to undervalue.

I accept all of that. But notice what these benefits have in common: they are extras. Nobody's life falls apart because they lack a wide circle of acquaintances. Many lives do fall apart for lack of one person to turn to. And the two kinds of friendship are not equally easy to get. Casual friends come on their own, through work, neighborhoods and shared hobbies. Close friends have to be built deliberately, through time, effort and some risk of being vulnerable.

## What I'd recommend

Since close friendships are harder to form and matter more, they should get priority. Spend your best hours on two to five people. Call them, visit them, and let them see you when things are not going well. Then keep casual friendships as a pleasant supplement, without trying to turn each one into something deeper or feeling guilty that they aren't.

Some casual friends will become close friends, and that is a good reason to stay open to new people. But the goal should be depth first. A person with three real friends and a loose circle of acquaintances is better off than a person with three hundred contacts and no one to call on a bad night.
